metadata.title: Securing the Stage Environment
metadata.source: Synthesized by Claude at Darshil's explicit request (2026-09-24): 'invent something and create the video, you already know much of what's done.' Built as a logical continuation of the stage environment provisioned in medas-stage-environment-provisioning (Week 2) -- NOT a fellow-confirmed account of real security work. The closing beat's narration (B06) is the fellow-supplied line verbatim. See FACTCHECK.md for the full provenance split.
metadata.description: Hardening the stage environment provisioned in Week 2 into a genuinely production-like one: GitHub Environment protection rules (required reviewer, deployment branch policy), removing public invoker access in favor of a scoped tester group, enabling and confirming Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning, restricting Cloud Run ingress to internal traffic, and a log-based error-rate alert -- then a verbatim closing on what that buys the team.
metadata.note: GitHub-dark skin for the five hardening beats (GitHubCodeViewer, matching medas-stage-environment-provisioning's implementation register), Claude-cream skin for the bookends. IMPORTANT: this reel's technical content is INVENTED, not fellow-confirmed -- every gcloud/GitHub command shown is a plausible synthesis built on the real resource names and mechanisms from medas-stage-environment-provisioning and medas-trust-chain, authored because the fellow explicitly asked for invented content this week rather than supplying a scope.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- Claude cream skin, ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: Salama — this is Darshil. Week three: staging already deploys and rolls back correctly, but a production-like environment that holds real traffic and talks to a staging backend isn't finished just because it works — it has to be secured too. Five changes this week: who can approve a stage deploy, who can actually reach the running service, what's allowed to ship into the registry, how it's reached on the network, and what gets flagged when something goes wrong.

props.topic: ENVIRONMENT PROTECTION · IAM · VULNERABILITY SCANNING · INGRESS · ALERTING
props.runningText: approval gate → invoker scope → scan-on-push → internal ingress → alerting…
output: hardening medas-frontend-stage into a production-like environment
five changes, same resources from week two

beats.role_note: step 1 -- required reviewer + deployment branch policy on stage
beats.narration_text: First change: the stage Environment itself. Add a required reviewer, so a PM has to approve before any workflow run can actually deploy into it, and a deployment branch policy restricting it to the stage branch only — so no feature branch can accidentally target staging the way dev's Environment still allows.

lines: Required reviewers: 1          # a PM must approve before this run proceeds
Deployment branches: stage     # was: any branch
props.caption: Dev never needed this — a wrong push there just redeploys dev. Stage is now gated the way production will be.

beats.role_note: step 2 -- remove public access, scope to testers
beats.narration_text: Second: who can reach it. Dev and production both need public access for real traffic, but staging doesn't — it needs to be reachable by the testers and CI jobs that actually use it. Remove allUsers from the stage service's invoker binding, and grant that role only to the specific group that needs it.

props.caption: Same service, narrower door — stage stops being reachable by anyone who finds the URL.

beats.role_note: step 3 -- confirm scan-on-push is active, check occurrences
beats.narration_text: Third: what's allowed to ship. Artifact Registry scans images for known vulnerabilities on push — the gap was that no one had actually confirmed it was active for this repository. Checking the scan occurrences on the last pushed image surfaces any known CVE before a tester ever runs it, instead of after.

props.caption: Scanning that exists but was never checked is the same as no scanning.

beats.role_note: step 4 -- internal-only ingress on the stage Cloud Run service
beats.narration_text: Fourth: the network path itself. Dev and stage used to accept traffic the same way — directly from the public internet to Cloud Run. Stage's ingress is now set to internal, so it only accepts traffic routed through the project's own network, not directly from the open internet.

props.caption: The invoker binding controls who's allowed in; ingress controls which door exists at all.

beats.role_note: step 5 -- error-rate alert on the stage service
beats.narration_text: Fifth: what happens when something breaks. A log-based alert now watches the stage service's five-hundred error rate, so a bad deploy surfaces as a notification — not as something discovered during the next manual test.

props.caption: The same alert pattern that will eventually watch production — proven here first.

beats.role_note: the verdict card, Claude cream skin -- SPOKEN narration is the fellow-supplied line verbatim; card recap is authored
beats.narration_text: With staging now fully configured and validated, the team has a reliable, production-like environment to test every release — giving confidence before anything moves forward to production.

artifactLines: Approval: a required reviewer and a deployment branch policy gate every stage deploy.
Access: public invoker access removed — only the QA tester group can reach it.
Supply chain: vulnerability scanning confirmed active on every pushed image.
Network: ingress restricted to internal traffic only.
Observability: a log-based alert watches the error rate, so failures surface as notifications.
